opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it was really the heart of the whole project, because "human quality" is a claim you have to earn. Smell is notoriously noisy. If you put the same molecule in front of two people, they'll often describe it pretty differently, and even the same person on two different days won't be perfectly consistent. So the bar isn't "match some ground-truth label." There isn't really a ground truth. The bar is: how well does a single trained human do at predicting what a panel of humans will say?

So we set it up like a head-to-head. We worked with a group of panelists who were trained, sort of like sommeliers for odor, on a shared vocabulary of descriptors like "fruity," "garlicky," "musky," "waxy," and on reference standards for each one so they were calibrated. Then we picked a set of molecules the model had never seen. Critically, these weren't just held-out rows from the training data. Many were new to the fragrance literature, so nobody could have memorized them. We had the panelists smell and rate each molecule, and separately we had the model predict ratings from structure alone.

The comparison asked whether the model's prediction landed closer to the panel's consensus than a typical individual panelist did. In other words, we treated the model as if it were just another person on the panel. On a bit more than half the molecules, the model was closer to the group average than the median panelist was. That's the sense in which we said it was performing at roughly human level. It's not superhuman, and it's not perfect, but it's in the same range as a trained person sitting in that room.

A couple of other things gave us confidence it was learning something real and not just a clever statistical trick. One was that the internal representation the model learned, what we started calling a principal odor map, organized molecules in a way that reflected perceptual similarity better than the standard chemical fingerprints people had used for decades. Molecules that smell alike sat near each other even when they looked structurally quite different. The other was that the map generalized to tasks it wasn't trained for, like predicting odor strength or relating to data from other species. When a representation transfers like that, it suggests you've captured something about the underlying biology and chemistry, not just the quirks of one dataset.

The deeper point for me is that the methodology had to respect how variable human perception is. If we'd just reported a correlation number against a label set, it wouldn't have meant much. Putting the model in the room alongside people and asking whether it could hold its own was the honest test.

r001.rationale: The response says the molecules were new to the model and many were new to fragrance literature, but does not state that no one had previously smelled them.

r002.rationale: It compares the model with individual panelists and says the model was closer than the median panelist on some molecules. It does not frame the test as whether adding the model improves the panel more than adding another person.

r003.rationale: The response reports that the model beat the median panelist on a bit more than half the molecules, not that it outperformed every individual panelist on average.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the question of "how good is good enough" is actually a really subtle one in olfaction, because unlike vision, where you can show someone a picture of a dog and basically everyone agrees it's a dog, people disagree about smells. A lot. If you hand two trained panelists the same molecule and ask them to describe it, one might say "grassy" and the other might say "green" or "cucumber," and they're both kind of right. So there's an inherent noise floor in the labels themselves.

And that turned out to be the key to answering the question. We realized we couldn't just ask "does the model match the humans," because the humans don't fully match each other. The right question was: is the model as close to the panel consensus as any individual trained human is?

So what we did was go out and collect a new dataset. We didn't want to just evaluate on the training distribution, because a lot of the public odor data comes from perfumery and flavor catalogs, and those molecules have been selected for being interesting or pleasant or commercially useful. We wanted molecules that had never been smelled and described before in a structured way. We worked with a panel of about fifteen people who we trained up over a few months on a fixed vocabulary of around fifty-five odor descriptors, things like "fruity," "fishy," "musky," "garlic," and so on. Then we gave them a few hundred novel molecules, ones that were, as far as we could tell, outside of anything the model had seen, and had them rate each molecule on every descriptor.

Then the comparison is pretty simple to describe. For each molecule, you take the mean of the panel, that's your consensus. You take one panelist out, and you ask how far that panelist's ratings are from the consensus of everyone else. That gives you a distribution of "how far off is a trained human, typically." And then you put the model in the same position: how far is the model's prediction from that same panel consensus?

And what we found was that the model was closer to the panel mean than the median panelist was, on a little more than half the molecules. So it's not that the model was superhuman in some magical sense. It's that if you lined it up alongside the panel and treated it like a sixteenth panelist, it would be a pretty good one. Somewhere in the middle of the pack, maybe a bit above. That's what we meant by human-level.

The other thing I'd add, because this mattered a lot to us, is that we looked carefully at where it failed. It wasn't random. There were descriptors like "musk" where the chemistry is genuinely hard, you've got very different structural classes that all smell musky, and the model struggled there in ways that actually tracked with how humans and chemists struggle too. And that gave us more confidence than the headline number, honestly. It wasn't just getting the easy ones right and the hard ones wrong in some arbitrary way; its mistakes looked like the mistakes a nose would make.

r001.rationale: The response says the panel rated novel molecules that had never been smelled and described in a structured way.

r002.rationale: It compares the model’s distance from panel consensus with individual panelists’ distance, but does not frame the test as whether adding the model improves the panel more than adding another person.

r003.rationale: It says the model was closer to the panel mean than the median panelist on a little more than half the molecules and describes it as around the middle of the pack; it does not say it outperformed every individual panelist on average.

astra-6.text:
The key was to test it on molecules that the model had never seen before and compare its predictions with what people actually smelled. That’s a little tricky, because people don’t all describe the same odor in exactly the same way. So human quality doesn’t mean matching every individual; you need to understand how much people agree with one another.

We had people smell the molecules and describe them, then compared the model’s predictions with the consensus of those descriptions. We could also compare each individual person with that same consensus. The question was: Is the model’s description about as close to the panel’s average description as an individual human’s is? That gives you a human benchmark, rather than just a machine-learning accuracy number.

r001.rationale: The response says the model had never seen the molecules; it does not say that no person had previously smelled them.

r002.rationale: It compares model predictions and individuals against the panel consensus, but does not frame the test as whether adding the model improves the panel more than adding another person.

r003.rationale: It says the model was about as close to the panel average as an individual human, not that it outperformed every individual panelist on average.

sol-6.1.text:
We had to compare the model against people on molecules it had never seen before. We selected a few hundred molecules and had a trained panel smell them and describe them using a fixed vocabulary—things like floral, fruity, grassy, or smoky. The model made predictions using only the molecular structures.

The important thing is that people don’t agree perfectly about smell. So we compared the model’s description to the panel average, and then asked how close each individual person came to that same average. The model was closer to the panel consensus than the typical panelist. That’s what we mean by human-level performance: on this task, its predictions were about as reliable as a person’s descriptions.

r001.rationale: It says the molecules were new to the model, but does not say no one had smelled them before.

r002.rationale: It compares the model and a typical panelist against panel consensus; it does not describe adding the model to the panel versus adding another person.

r003.rationale: It says the model was closer to consensus than the typical panelist, not that it outperformed every individual panelist on average.
